headline: 4:52 AM max ebb: the only window that mattered this week
subhead: Daytime current in the Canal is producing bait movement without bass commitment — the real bite is happening before the sun's up and after it's down.
body_markdown:
4:52 AM. That's when max ebb hit the east end Tuesday morning, and that's when I put two fish over thirty inches in the net off the Herring Run rocks before the sky even started to gray up. Both came on an olive Savage Gear sand eel, swimming it with the current instead of against it, letting the rip do the work. By 6:15, with the sun up and the current still running strong but the light flooding the water, it was over. Dead over. That's the story of the Canal right now and it's been the story for about two weeks — the tide's doing exactly what it should, the current's got plenty of push, but the bass have gone nocturnal on us the same way they have from the Jersey shore up through the Sound.

I've fished this ditch thirty years and I can tell you the current itself hasn't changed a bit. East end still turns on hard around the top of the ebb, that rip line stacking up off the Route 6 bridge piling and running out toward the tower, same as it's done every July of my life. West end's still setting up its current seam off the Mashnee flats on the flood, pushing bait into that eddy on the inside of the bend. The mechanics are all there. What's changed is the water's warmed up enough — surface temps pushing into the low 70s the way they have coastwide — that the stripers don't want to commit to those seams under a bright July sun. They're doing what bass do everywhere right now: sliding down, going quiet in the heat, and turning it back on when the light drops out.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the bite would stay tide-dependent with the best windows on max ebb and max flood as bait gets funneled through — and that's exactly what's playing out, just compressed into a smaller clock than usual. The difference this week is timing. It's not enough anymore to just hit max current during daylight. You need max current AND low light, and right now in late July those two things only overlap for about ninety minutes at each end of the day, plus the night tides in between.

Night fishing has been the better program, honestly. I had a report from a guy working the Sagamore side around midnight Sunday who did well on eels — bridled, drifted through the seam under the Sagamore Bridge on the last two hours of the ebb, three fish in the mid-30s, one that pushed 20 pounds released after a quick photo. That's the kind of quality that's still in this system. It hasn't left. It's just gone underground, or under-dark, however you want to put it.

Scusset Beach side has been decent for the bluefish crowd, and that's tracking with what's happening everywhere else on this coast right now — bunker have been getting pushed into the east end approach by the same bait movement that's got blues blitzing from the Cape Cod Bay side down through Buzzards. Guys throwing Deadly Dicks and Hopkins spoons off the rocks at Scusset during the last hour of the flood have been into blues steady, 3 to 6 pounds, occasional bigger fish mixed in. That bite's been more reliable during daylight than the bass have, which tells you something about how sun-shy the stripers have gotten.

Fluke have been a west end story, mostly around Mashnee Island and down toward Phinneys Harbor, working the deeper cuts on the tail of the ebb when the water's clean and moving but not screaming. Nothing huge — most fish 16 to 19 inches, a few keepers mixed in on white Gulp Swimming Mullets tipped on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom where the current softens against the channel edge. It's a pick, not a program, but it's there if you want a change of pace between bass tides.

No albies or bonito through the Canal yet, and I don't expect them to show here first — this isn't their water, not really, though Buzzards Bay and the Vineyard corridor are exactly the kind of leading-edge zones where I'd expect the season's first scout fish to show given how the water's trending. If that happens down there in the next few days, don't be surprised if a stray albie shows up chasing bait through the east end on a hot flood tide later in the season. It's happened before. Not this week though.

Moon's swinging toward the new moon early next week, which means the currents are going to build back up after sitting on this softer neap stretch — I called that softening last week and it's held, current speeds down maybe 10-15% off a full spring tide. When the new moon current kicks back in, that funnel effect through both ends gets stronger, which should concentrate bait harder and give the bass a more defined reason to commit even during marginal light. If I had one window to fish this weekend, I'd take the pre-dawn max ebb Saturday at the east end — should be running around 5:10 AM — and I'd have an eel rigged and ready before the current even reaches full strength. Get there early, because once that rip lays down, the window's closed and you're just watching water go by.
